notes.short: The LORD's great army: an allegory, some read
notes.about: Joel pictures the Day of the LORD coming with a vast army that sweeps the land. They look like horses, charge like mighty men, scale walls and enter houses like thieves, and the LORD calls them His army. Some read it as an allegory: the locust swarm pictures God's judgments, or invading armies.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: a great and strong army appears
figure.means: as some read it, the locust host standing for God's judgments or for invading armies: terrible, not to be resisted, reaching everywhere

notes.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes' Notes) says the imagery is taken from locusts, and the allegory is so complete that warriors, horses and war are in part meant; its object is the order and course of God's judgments. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) takes the locusts as only symbols of human foes, first the Assyrian host and at last the final antichristian league.
notes.limit: Scholars differ. Others take these verses as a plague of real locusts, likened to an army, and not as an allegory. Those who read an allegory differ on what it pictures: God's judgments in general, or Assyria and later foes.

cites.quote: The imagery throughout these verses is taken from the flight and inroad of locusts. The allegory is so complete, that the prophet compares them to those things which are, in part, intended under them, warriors, horses and instruments of war ... The object of the allegory is to describe the order and course of the divine judgments; how they are terrific, irresistible, universal, overwhelming

cites.quote: understanding, however, that the locusts are only the symbols of human foes. The immense Assyrian host of invaders under Sennacherib (compare Isa 37:36 ) destroyed by God ( Joe 2:18 , Joe 2:20-21 ), may be the primary objects of the prophecy; but ultimately the last antichristian confederacy, destroyed by special divine interposition, is meant

notes.about: The second line says the first again in other words: they charge like mighty men, they scale the walls like men of war.

lines.words: they scale the walls like men of war.

notes.evidence: Lowth gives this verse among his examples of synonymous parallel lines, and says such lines are made of synonymous terms, sometimes three or more and sometimes two.

cites.quote: Like mighty men shall they rush on; Like warriors shall they mount the wall: ... Joel, ii. 7. ... In the foregoing examples may be observed the different degrees of Synonymous Parallelism. The Parallel Lines sometimes consist of three or more Synonymous terms; sometimes of two

notes.short: Heavens and earth, then the earth and the heavens
notes.about: Wonders are promised in the heavens and on the earth. The blood, fire and smoke may be the wonders on the earth, and the darkened sun and the moon turned to blood the wonders in the heavens, so the two come back in reverse order.

lines.words: I will show wonders in the heavens
blood and fire and columns of smoke.
The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood

notes.evidence: Boys suspects the same distinct resumption of separate topics in Joel: the changes in the sun and moon, in the last line, seem to be the wonders in the heavens of the first, and what the third line speaks of seems to be the wonders in the earth of the second.

cites.quote: I suspect the same distinct resumption of separate topics in the prophet Joel. ... The changes in the sun and moon, spoken of in a., seem to be the wonders in the heavens, predicted in a.; ... in b., the wonders in the earth, predicted in b.
